meaningMnemonic: This is a demon . He's got that classic demon look to him: wild fangs, a devilish tongue sticking out, and the horn on his head. There's also a little flame near him because you can't get up to demonic activities without a little fire!

What's this radical, you ask? It's leather ! Meet the leather man decked out in an all-leather getup. He's wearing a leather cowboy hat, a leather vest, a leather belt, and he's even holding leather reins.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means mix .
This is the left side of the kanji 朝 , so we'll call it morning too.

This is the restaurant radical. Do you see the moody light fixture shining down on a steel cloche, itself sitting atop a table covered with a white tablecloth? C'mon, you've gotta treat yourself to a nice dinner here and there!
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means road .
This radical looks like the kind of vines you usually see hanging from trees in the jungle. Imagine swinging on these Tarzan style. "AaaaAA aAA AAAaaaa!"

There's going to be a tsunami . So you get up on your roof . You see people across the street , in a rice paddy . They watch as you put on a pair of fins . And you begin acting . This is your last chance to perform ! Hints But why? Because this acting will distract everyone from the impending tsunami. You dance around in your fins, pretending to swim. It's a wonderful performance.
readingMnemonic: As the acting en ds ( えん ), so do you all. Hints The performance and the tsunami end together. How poetic.

meaningMnemonic: A mouth that wants peace can call for it. If you don’t have a mouth, you can’t call for peace. So use your mouth and call for peace when you can. Peace is great. Hints Call for peace. Say it aloud. I’m using my mouth to call for peace!
readingMnemonic: But before you call for peace, you must first placate the masses. To do so, you astound them with your yo -yo ( よ ) skills. Once they are so entranced by how talented you are with a yo-yo, you easily convince them to make peace. Hints Imagine yourself whirling this yo-yo about while you call for peace. Imagine yourself doing a variety of tricks with it as you slowly convince the people to agree to peace.

meaningMnemonic: From the top of a mountain you see something that looks like a big lip ring jutting out into the ocean: it's a cape ! You know, the geological formation where a big piece of land sticks out into the ocean? That kind of cape. Hints Cape Cod, for example. Picture it now (or look it up if you need to). Really does look like a big lip ring stuck in the side of Massachusetts, doesn't it? Imagine seeing that cape from the top of your mountain, wind blustering around you.
readingMnemonic: Looking down at the cape , you realize capes always make the coastline look jagged, like a saw or key ( さき ). Thanks for keeping the coastline interesting, you saw-key capes! Hints Try to draw that bit of coastline where the cape is. Nice, easy, smooth lines, until BAM! — the cape. Now the coastline is all jagged like the edge of a saw or key.

meaningMnemonic: Moving in the direction of a gun , an alligator can carry out a murder once it reaches it. This alligator wants to kill someone. The alligator wants to carry out their execution. Hints See the alligator swim really slowly in the direction of a gun. See the alligator as it prepares to carry out the murder. It’s scary.
readingMnemonic: In order to carry out this murder, the alligator has to sneak up on its prey, so it can shoot it. You look across the water and see a shee p ( し ) grazing by the shore. The alligator is going to carry out a murder on that sheep! Hints Watch as the alligator slinks under the water, holding the gun above the water. When it gets close enough, it carries out the murder on the sheep. Shooting it right in the chest. Now it can eat the sheep without worrying about needing to chomp on it.

meaningMnemonic: Dirt can become a castle at any time. You just have to have the right conditions. The right time, the right people, and any patch of dirt can grow into a huge castle. Hints Every great building, especially castles, started off as just a plot of dirt, you know? It's kind of inspiring what we can become.
readingMnemonic: Once you turn dirt into a castle , that's all she wro te ( しろ ). That's it. It's done. The story is over. Hints Once a castle is there, there's really no turning back. So just remember that when dirt becomes a castle, that's all she wrote.

meaningMnemonic: They say that flowers held by a turkey on a stool are good to defend yourself with. Even better than a guard dog they say. People are so confused by the turkey sitting on a stool holding flowers that they just lose their will to fight. This turkey is great to defend yourself and your home. Hints Picture this turkey holding its flowers while sitting on its stool. Hear it gobbling as it defends everything around it with its mere presence.
readingMnemonic: The only thing this flower-bearing turkey can't defend against is Go dzilla ( ご ). Godzilla is pretty much undefeatable, especially for a turkey. The turkey is totally unable to defend anything from the mighty Godzilla. Hints Imagine Godzilla approaching the flower turkey. Hear Godzilla roar as the turkey gobbles in fear before being crushed beneath the massive and scaly foot of Godzilla.

meaningMnemonic: The demon radical and the demon kanji are exactly the same! Wicked!
readingMnemonic: How do you keep a demon locked up? Use a key ( き ). Use a lock and key and keep that demon locked up safely behind bars so he can’t get out and do bad demon stuff. Hints Picture yourself locking up a demon with a special demon containing key. Hear the key click into the lock as the demon screams to be set free.

meaningMnemonic: A roof falls on you right between your rib cage and your mouth , slicing through you like a knife and managing to completely divide your body in two. Hints Imagine the shock you feel as you look down and see this massive fallen roof dividing your body in two between the mouth and rib cage. Of all the places to get divided in two, the rib cage-to-mouth region is by far one of the worst.
readingMnemonic: Who caused this roof to fall on you and divide your body in two? Wari o ( わり ) and his wa lrus ( わ ) sidekick. Wario's always been a bad guy, but since teaming up with his walrus buddy, he's gotten into some really twisted stuff… like using roofs to divide people in half, guillotine-style. Hints Why did Wario and his walrus choose you, of all people, to divide in two? They were after your fortune. Now that you're out of the way, they're planning to divide it up amongst themselves, fifty-fifty.

meaningMnemonic: If you mix different types of power you'll produce something effective . Hints It doesn't matter what power you mix, because all power is strong. No matter what you use this mixed power on, it will be effective. Try to imagine some situations where you'd use it, and what effects it might have.
readingMnemonic: The most effective mix of two powers is two こう いち s. Pair them up, and their powers will mix to incredible effect. Now use them to attack some animal-like creature. It's super effective! Hints The two こういち s' double punch attack was super effective against that Pikurchort.

meaningMnemonic: Reaching your ear is the sound of a drunkard who can’t find employment . You hear him before you see him because he’s behind some trash cans. Being a drunkard, he’s like, super wasted and just kind of rambling to himself, making strange sounds. No wonder he can’t find employment. Hints Hear the strange sounds this drunkard is making. Let his ramblings enter your ears and imagine what he could be trying to say.
readingMnemonic: Since this guy is such a pathetic drunkard, it comes as no shock ( しょく ) that he can’t find employment . If he did find employment, I would be filled with both shock and awe. Hints Actually you find out that he does have employment. He’s a garbage man. Feel the shock of making this shocking discovery. How can this drunkard possibly hold down his job like this?

meaningMnemonic: If you can eat grain s while running up stairs , you'll excel at everything. Hints This special workout routine is so hard that, if you can do it, you'll be able to excel at every other thing you try.
readingMnemonic: In order to excel at this, though, you need a good pair of shoe s ( しゅう ). Hints You have to eat the grains AND run up the stairs, or you aren't actually excelling. Good shoes will help you get there faster and protect your toes.

meaningMnemonic: Dirt shifts direction in winter , and instead of the usual stuff it starts to grow shellfish that are very extravagant . These shellfish are so extravagant because they can only be grown in the dirt in winter (after the dirt has shifted "direction" and started sustaining shellfish instead of plants, that is). Hints Imagine tasting this incredible extravagance. Shellfish normally have a briny flavor, but these ones have earthy notes. Earthy shellfish?! I've never heard of something so extravagant. Try to imagine that extravagant, expensive flavor on your tongue.
readingMnemonic: To make this experience even more extravagant , you eat them with a zei ber ( ぜい ), a German saber. A fork is just too plain for these extravagant shellfish — you gotta use a zeiber for maximum extravagance. Hints Imagine trying to use a zeiber to skewer an extravagant shellfish, then raise it to your mouth. You probably cut your lips a little bit, to be honest. It's all very impractical, but that's what it means to be extravagant.

meaningMnemonic: A leader wishing to stop criminal s will write a moving haiku . The leader pleads with the criminals to stop their crimes, to look within, and to realize there's more to life (like poetry!). Hints Unfortunately, the leader of the criminals also writes haiku, and they want all the criminals to keep doing crimes. Look inside and see how much you want what others have, write a haiku, and then steal!
readingMnemonic: A haiku is still a hai ku ( はい ). Whether it's written by a law abiding leader or a criminal leader. Hints Just remember: a haiku is always a haiku.

meaningMnemonic: The leader of the restaurant says, " Halt !" to everyone who wants to come in. The leader looks them up and down. Stares into their eyes. And then, maybe, they may go into the restaurant to eat. Hints Imagine being told to halt in front of your favorite restaurant, then being turned away. Noooo! Better start sucking up to the restaurant leader.
readingMnemonic: People only halt because they want this restaurant's world famous ta ter ( てい ) tots. Which is probably why there is a leader out front making sure only people who can really appreciate the tater tots can get in to eat them. Hints HALT! NO TATERS FOR YOU!

meaningMnemonic: You need to go up on the roof and use it like a slide seven times to make this your house . A house isn't a home until you've slid down its roof exactly seven times, you know. Hints Imagine staring down at the ground as you prepare to use the roof of your house like a slide. I hope you aren't afraid of heights, because you have to do this seven times in a row.
readingMnemonic: When you slide down the roof of your house , you end up with a tack ( たく ) in your butt cheek. All the roof shingles on your new home are attached with tacks, so it's honestly a miracle that you only got one tack stuck in you. Hints Feel the tack stab into your butt as you slide down your house's roof. Ow! Weirdly, though, it kinda makes you feel more at one with the house — like it's really your home now.

meaningMnemonic: The sick sheep is itchy and it can barely sit still. Help the poor sheep! Hints Imagine you were itchy but you couldn't scratch the spot. Now that you know how the sick sheep feels, give it a hand!
readingMnemonic: Even though the sheep is itchy , look how kah-yu te ( かゆ ) it is! It’s not just cute. It’s kah-yute! Hints Say it out loud! Kah-yuuute!

meaningMnemonic: You place a cross on this drunkard 's clothes to show him you judge him. In fact, you yell, "I JUDGE YOU FOR BEING DRUNK AND WEARING THESE CLOTHES, TAKE THIS!" Hints He yells back, "YOU CAN'T JUDGE ME, I CAN DO WHAT I WANT. GET THAT JUDGEY CROSS OFF ME!"
readingMnemonic: As you judge each other, your cy borg ( さい ) comes stomping over and slams the drunkard against the wall. With your trusty cyborg coming to your rescue, you can continue to judge this guy all you want. Hints The cyborg joins in, "A judge would convict you if the fashion police brought you in. I have a bunch of meat and robot parts and even I'm better looking than you."

meaningMnemonic: Loiter ing around with a brush ? Sorry, but you're breaking the law . If you have a brush, that's okay. If you're loitering, that's okay. If you combine the two? Well... watch your back. Hints Imagine a police officer coming for you. He's yelling at you because you have a brush and you're loitering. He grabs you, throws you to the ground, telling you what you're doing wrong.
readingMnemonic: Where were you loitering with your brush, breaking the law ? Right outside the Ritz ( りつ ) Hotel. You'd think that it would be okay since you were staying there, but the law is the law. Hints Imagine the hotel staff watching as you get thrown to the ground. You yell "won't the Ritz do anything to help me??" They won't.

meaningMnemonic: Take this road 's measurement . Hmm. It seems a bit too long. As you measure it, you continue down this road, wondering where it will lead you. Hints Roads are really long, so I imagine it would take a long time to measure it (if you want to go from end to end). Imagine yourself pulling a tape measure along with you, all the while thinking, "Where will this lead me?”
readingMnemonic: Where does the road that you're measuring lead to? To a dou ghnut ( どう ) shop! Hints What a perfect way to end this road measuring. You're hungry. Nom nom nom. Imagine eating your fill, and taste the doughnuts in your mouth. You just walked a long way!

meaningMnemonic: The leather radical and the leather kanji are exactly the same! Cool!
readingMnemonic: One way to get leather is to skin a male chicken, a cock ( かく ). Not a very efficient way to get leather, but one way nonetheless. Hints You won’t get much leather from a cock, but you could skin one in a pinch, should you really need a little extra leather.

meaningMnemonic: Giving cleat s to a child carrying an umbrella is the best way to gather milk . You don't have any containers, so the child has to hold milk in the upside-down umbrella. The cleats are so the child can run back and forth to transport the milk around. Hints See this child running in his cleats. Picture him holding the umbrella upside-down, milk sloshing all about as he runs.
readingMnemonic: But where is this child exactly? He’s in New ( にゅう ) York City. What’s he doing in New York City you ask? Well, he's milking a cow. Why is there a cow to be milked in New York City? Good question. It’s the end of the world and New York City is the last remaining civilization. This is how people live now. Milk is important. Hints Imagine post-apocalyptic New York City. Milk is a hot commodity here so it’s important not to spill any of the milk. Imagine yourself carrying the milk in the umbrella and being careful not to spill any of it.

meaningMnemonic: Wrap vines around a stool to obtain it. Don't worry about paying for it, sneak into the stool store and tie some vines around the legs. Then when you leave, pull the vines and the stool will come out after. That's how you obtain a stool! Hints You can obtain a lot of goods this way without needing any cash. Just don't tell anyone I told you.
readingMnemonic: Today you want to obtain a new pair of shoe s ( しゅう ). You tie your vines around the stool they're on, and slowly inch them toward the door. Hints You have to pull very slowly, or the shoes will fall off the stool. But you really, really want to obtain these particular shoes (they're really sweet), so you keep scooting them toward you.

meaningMnemonic: When your sick mama tries to do a task she's filled with pain ! Hints Sick people shouldn't have to do things, of course they're in pain. You shouldn't let your mama do anything if she's in pain, do it for her!
readingMnemonic: Your mama's pain is too ( つう ) much for her to handle, so now you have to do all of her tasks too. Hints You finish doing your tasks and hers too, and you ask her, "How is the pain now, Mama?" "THE PAIN IS TOO MUCH!" she cries. Oh mama.

meaningMnemonic: The king can see the present time for what it really is. The future isn't important. The past isn't important. The present is when everything appear s. Hints People are constantly asking the king to do things for them and solve their problems. But the king can see exactly what needs to be done at the present time, and what can wait until tomorrow.
readingMnemonic: At the present time the king is Gen ji ( げん ). The time has finally come for him to get serious, and as they say, there's no time like the present. Hints Picture pretty Genji, carefully instructing his followers what to do at the present time and what can wait.

meaningMnemonic: The leader put flowers on a cliff . That is their task . It is to provide and equip the cliff with flowers. Hints Imagine a leader carrying flowers up to the top of a cliff. They are saying "I must provide more flowers to the cliff" as they climb up.
readingMnemonic: Why do they provide and equip the cliff with flowers? It's all for the bee s ( び ). Hints "The bees must be equipped with more flowers. I will provide these flowers for the bees!"

meaningMnemonic: You stop a spoon from moving by tying it with thread that's purple . The spoon wouldn't stop moving around, so you had to use your favorite purple thread to make it stop. It's the strongest thread you have. Hints Imagine tying this spoon down with thread that's a color other than purple. Ah, the thread snaps. Darn, you better use your extra strong purple thread (the best color for strength!).
readingMnemonic: To remember this reading, think about how the village you previously went to was all purple . It was the " 村先 " ( むらさき ) that you went to. Hints Imagine that everything is in purple in this village. Cars, houses, trees. Absolutely everything was purple.

meaningMnemonic: A shellfish with a knife makes all the rule s. It isn't supposed to be making rules, but it has a knife, so who's going to argue? Hints Picture a shellfish wielding a knife and shouting out new rules to all of the nervous people standing around it.
readingMnemonic: The first rule the shellfish enacts is that all humans take off their sock s ( そく ) and give them to him. Hmm... is this some kind of nasty shellfish? Who would want socks? Hints Once everyone follows the rule, and the shellfish is on top of a pile of socks, he cackles, "It's easier to stab your toes with my knife now! Let's get to more rules!"

meaningMnemonic: Take a tree and make two moon -shaped shelf units with it. Moon radical-shaped, that is. Those moon radicals standing side by side kinda look like a shelf, don't you think? The tree on the left is just there to remind you it's made of wood, I guess. A lovely wooden shelf. Hints Imagine having some tall, moon radical-shaped shelves in your house. Where would you put them? Picture them there now. Honestly, they'd actually look pretty sophisticated.
readingMnemonic: To match the moon radical shape, this would have to be a pretty tall shelf , meaning you can store a ton-a -stuff ( たな ) on it. Hints Think about the ton-a-stuff you're going to put on this tall shelf. Like, literally measure out a ton of things and put them on there. It can hold it, I'm sure…

meaningMnemonic: How do you make a hole nice and big ? You gotta stab something in it. Just thrust it right in there. And make sure your movements are really sudden . Stabs and thrusts are more effective when they're sudden. Hints Yeah, take that, you hole! Stab, thrust, stab! Wow, this hole keeps getting bigger thanks to all your stabbin'.
readingMnemonic: Give that hole one last big stab , now you've totes ( とつ ) showed that hole who's boss. What did I tell you about the sudden thrust technique? It's totes super effective. Like, totes. Hints Remember "totes," that slang word for "totally"? It fell out of use almost as sudden as it appeared. Now it totes gives me a little stab of nostalgia whenever I hear it.

meaningMnemonic: Riding a tsunami you see a turkey carrying a cross , but that’s pretty standard here. This is your dreamland. You always dream about tsunamis and the turkeys carrying crosses that ride them. This might be strange for other people, but for you it’s pretty normal. Hints See this tsunami riding turkey in your mind. Hear it gobble loudly as it waves its cross around. Remember, this is standard fare for you. Nothing unusual here.
readingMnemonic: These wacky dreams are only standard fare in June ( じゅん ) though. You don’t have them any other time of the year, just in June. You don’t know why June is the only time you have dreams about tsunami riding turkeys, but that’s just the way it is. Hints It’s usually pretty toasty in the month of June (in the Northern Hemisphere, at least) so imagine going to bed in this heat. Feel the spray of the refreshing tsunami water in your dream as the turkey continues to ride those tsunami waves with his cross.

meaningMnemonic: You have a bow and you want to make it long . To do that, you'd naturally just stretch it. Hints Imagine holding this bow in your hands, and then stretching it into a longer bow. Feel the strain on your arms as you try to stretch wood. You can feel it stretching, but it's strenuous.
readingMnemonic: As you stretch the bow, you hear someone running at you. "That's my bow you're stretching!" yells Mrs. Chou ( ちょう ). She is not happy that you're stretching her things. You should probably try to un-stretch it, put it down, and run before she beats you. Hints Now Mrs. Chou is hitting you with the stretched out bow. You cry and apologize, but she won't listen. "I'm going to stretch you, like you stretched my bow," she says. Then she does it.

meaningMnemonic: The leader of a hundred forehead s in the heart of winter is superior at being gentle . These hundred foreheads are sensitive, especially in the heart of winter, so the leader must be very gentle. Not just any kind of gentle though—the superior kind of gentle that will keep a hundred foreheads following. Hints As a leader, you are superior. You’re so gentle to these foreheads. See yourself caring for them in the winter. Feel the chill in the air as you wrap the foreheads in blankets and prepare heating pads for them.
readingMnemonic: You need to be superior because all of these foreheads belong to you ths ( ゆう ). They don't know how to take care of themselves, though they try to convince you they can. They're too young to know any better. Hints Picture the youths trying to show you that they are the superior ones, then they sneeze, their eyes fill with tears, and you have to gently tuck them back into bed. Silly youths.

meaningMnemonic: A tsunami of shrimp crashes into a swamp . Now the swamp is filled with shrimp. They used to live in the ocean, but the tsunami has carried them to their new home in the swamp. Hints Imagine yourself in the swamp when the tsunami hits. Feel the water crash into you along with the shrimp. You’re all wet and shrimpy now.
readingMnemonic: Your house was right next to the swamp and on this side of your house you had many a tack ( たく ) there to hang things on. Now, on every tack there is skewered a shrimp. The force of the tsunami drove them into the tacks on the side of your house. Hints Look at the side of your house. It’s covered with shrimp that have been impaled on the tacks. Perfect for dinner.

meaningMnemonic: A drop of water falls from a bear onto the ground and needs to be wiped up with a towel . Only a teacher or an expert could get away with getting close to this wet bear to wipe up after it. Hints The expert is also your teacher, and she's showing you how to clean up after this bear.
readingMnemonic: The teacher tells you to start with something smaller, after all, you're not an expert yet. You have to practice on a wet shee p ( し ). "I became a wet, dangerous animal expert by starting with sheep, you will too!" your teacher says. Hints Your teacher assures you this wet sheep is far less dangerous to clean up after than a wet bear. They're the expert, so you should listen and wipe up after that sheep.

meaningMnemonic: In the morning , if you want your hat to dry , you need to hang it on a tree trunk . In the morning, everything is covered in dew. The grass is wet, the leaves are wet, but the tree trunk isn't wet! It was protected by the rest of the tree, so you can hang your hat there to dry. Hints Picture everything early in the morning covered in damp dew. Even your hat is uncomfortably wet. Now walk up to a large tree trunk and touch it—it's dry!
readingMnemonic: You lean against the tree trunk , waiting for your hat to dry, and suddenly you realize Genghis Khan ( かん ) is on the other side of it. You look around and see that all of the tree trunks around you have Mongols drying their hats under them. Hints Now that you think about it, Genghis Khan was the one who taught people that tree trunks stay dry in the morning!

meaningMnemonic: Put your hand over your eye to watch over others. Hints You know that way cartoon characters and pirates watch out below them, with their hand shading their eye? That! Now imagine doing that right now.
readingMnemonic: As you watch over your friends and neighbors you see movement in the distance. Oh no, it's Genghis Khan ( かん ) and his army! Hints Welp, nothing much watching over them will do now. Genghis Khan is probably going to take over your town, so I guess you can watch if you want but... I wouldn't.

meaningMnemonic: You suck something in and obtain it. Shhheewwwwww! When you suck something in and obtain it into your body, you have done absorption because it's been sucked inside of you.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 若者の知識の吸収スピードにはついていけないよ。
sentences.english: I can't keep up with the speed at which young people absorb knowledge.

sentences.japanese: うちの手ぬぐいは、水分の吸収力がすごいんです。
sentences.english: Our tenugui absorbs a great deal of liquid.

sentences.japanese: 植物が水分を取り入れる時って、どれくらいのスピードで吸収するんですか？
sentences.english: When plants get water, how long does it take for them to absorb it?

sentences.japanese: 生理の日を快適に過ごすなら、より吸収量の多いナプキンを選ぶのがおすすめです。
sentences.english: If you want to be comfortable on your menstrual days, we recommend choosing a pad with a higher absorption rate.

meaningMnemonic: Your performance skill allows you to be great at acting and doing awesome performance s.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 表情で演技ができる役者を目指しています。
sentences.english: I aspire to be an actor who can convey emotions through facial expressions.

sentences.japanese: フグは大学で演技の勉強をしています。
sentences.english: Fugu is studying acting at university.

sentences.japanese: あの女優の演技力は素晴らしい。
sentences.english: That actress’s acting ability is magnificent.

meaningMnemonic: A superior haiku requires someone really famous and well known to read it... it's just on that level. Who is super well known and who deserves to read this superior haiku? A great actor , perhaps?
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: あの俳優は、態度に問題がある。
sentences.english: That actor has a real attitude problem.

sentences.japanese: その女優は、いつも大物俳優に尻尾をふっているため、他の女優から嫌われている。
sentences.english: That actress is always fawning over big actors, so other actresses don't like her.

sentences.japanese: 私の恋人は、この芝居で馬の役を演じている俳優よ。
sentences.english: My boyfriend is the actor performing the part of the horse in this play.

meaningMnemonic: A man who is superior to us is an actor , or more specifically a male actor . Just a word of warning: over the years this word has taken on the connotation of "adult film actor" so most people would use 俳優 for "actor" now. You'll be learning that word very soon!
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: あの男優、ファンに対する態度がひどいので有名だよ。
sentences.english: That actor is famous for his terrible attitude toward his fans.

sentences.japanese: あ、それって、二作目の映画で有名になった男優だよね。
sentences.english: Oh, that's the actor who became famous for his second movie, right?

sentences.japanese: その俳優は新人の時から、「主演男優賞を狙いたい」と真面目に語っていた。
sentences.english: From the time he was a newcomer, that actor had expressed his sincere desire to win the Best Actor award.

meaningMnemonic: The present time is the time you're actually in. You aren't really in any other time, because that's not how time works!
readingMnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!

sentences.japanese: 現にさっきそう言ったじゃありませんか。
sentences.english: Didn’t you actually say that a while ago?

sentences.japanese: 現に人が死んでるっていうのに、よくそんなことが言えますね。
sentences.english: Some people were actually killed. How can you say such a thing?

sentences.japanese: 現にこの瞬間にも飢餓で苦しんでいる人がいるんですよ？
sentences.english: There are actually people suffering from starvation at this very moment, you know.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji means come to an end , so the verb vocab version is also about something ending: it means to be finished or to be done . 済む is used when something finishes or is resolved, often without further trouble, like 支払いが済む (the payment is completed). From this core idea of resolution, it also pops up in various other expressions about things coming to a close or being "enough." For example, 気が済む means to feel satisfied with something such that you can get some issue out of your system, as in 気が済むまで泣く (cry till you feel better). Likewise, 〜で済む expresses that something on its own is sufficient, like 電話一本で済む (a single phone call is all it takes).

You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: If something isn't done and you want it to be finished , your best bet is to sue ( す ) someone. meaningMnemonic: The kanji means mix , and you already learned its transitive and intransitive pair: 混ぜる (to mix) and 混ざる (to get mixed). 混じる is another intransitive verb, but it means to be mixed in with . So how are 混ざる and 混じる different? 混ざる is used to talk about things that become mixed together as part of the same whole — like blended colors or intermingled groups. 混じる , on the other hand, is less about blending smoothly and more about something getting mixed in when it doesn't quite belong — static in your audio, scattered strands of gray in your dark hair, or even some random stranger sitting at your group's table. You can remember this by thinking about how this out-of-place thing getting mixed in makes you want to jeer ( じる ): "Boo, get out of here! You don't fit in!"

sentences.japanese: いつか俺も自分の家を建てたいな。
sentences.english: Someday I want to build my own house too.

sentences.japanese: 大きな橋を建てるにはエンジニアが必要です。
sentences.english: Building a big bridge requires engineers.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means call so the verb vocab version is to call or to call out . As in "HEY, YOU!"
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the kanji, so you should be good here. Just imagine yourself  calling out to someone: " YO ( よ )! You!"

sentences.japanese: タクシーを呼んでもらえますか？
sentences.english: Could you call a taxi for me?

sentences.japanese: 空港で、見知らぬ人に名前を大声で呼ばれた。
sentences.english: A stranger suddenly called out my name at the airport.

sentences.japanese: 彼はあなたの命の恩人なんだから、誕生日会に呼んだ方がいいわよ。
sentences.english: He saved your life so you should invite him to your birthday party.

meaningMnemonic: 確認 is confirmation. When that's a verb, you have to confirm or to verify .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will help immensely if you know the word 確認 already as well.

sentences.japanese: 警察には、情報をリアルタイムで確認するシステムがある。
sentences.english: The police have a system to verify information in real time.

sentences.japanese: 弁護士に確認してみた方がいいんじゃない？
sentences.english: Wouldn't it be better to confirm with a lawyer?

sentences.japanese: 我が社がついに赤字を脱したことを確認した時、私は胸を撫で下ろしました。
sentences.english: I was so relieved when I confirmed that our company finally got out of the red.

meaningMnemonic: To preserve and defend something is to conserve and to protect . I won't let you destroy this land I'm trying to protect !
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 自然を保護するために、何ができるか考えてみましょう。
sentences.english: Let's think about what we can do to conserve nature.

sentences.japanese: 警察は新宿駅近辺を一人で歩いていた少女を保護した。
sentences.english: The police took the girl who was wandering by herself near Shinjuku Station into protective custody.

sentences.japanese: あそこで虫をついばんでいる鳥は、国際間で保護することが取り決められた鳥です。
sentences.english: The bird pecking at insects over there is a species that is protected under international agreements.

meaningMnemonic: 批判 is criticism so the verb version of that would be to criticize .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will be much easier to read this if you know 批判 , as well.

sentences.japanese: 私の彼は、私を批判すると、いつも後でアメをくれる。
sentences.english: My boyfriend always gives me a hard candy after criticizing me.

sentences.japanese: みんなは口をそろえて男のことを批判した。
sentences.english: Everyone said the same thing and criticized the man.

sentences.japanese: お前って、他人の批判してばっかりだよな。
sentences.english: You're always finding fault with other people, aren't you?

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means cut off so the verb vocab version is to cut off . This is often used metaphorically to describe cutting off things that tie us down mentally or societally. This includes ending bad habits, so it also means to quit doing something . Don't confuse this with 断る which means "to refuse." You know this is to cut off because of the つ , which hints that you have had two ( つ ) too many chocolates, and it's time to cut you off.
readingMnemonic: URGH! The reading isn't even the same as 断る , how frustrating. to cut off is read as たつ . Instead of eating too many chocolates and getting cut off, maybe you're eating too many tater tots ( たつ ). Don't eat so many of those, it's unhealthy. You have to cut off tater tots from your diet so you don't get fat.

sentences.japanese: これでもう逃げ道は断たれてしまった。
sentences.english: This means that there's no longer any way to escape.

sentences.japanese: お酒とタバコを断つべきだってのは、自分でも分かってます。医者にも断つように言われたんですが、すぐには無理ですよ。
sentences.english: I know that I should cut out alcohol and cigarettes. My doctor also told me to cut them out, but there’s no way I could do so right away.

sentences.japanese: あの時は、はらわたを断つ思いで別れを告げたんだ。
sentences.english: At that time, I said goodbye with a gut-wrenching feeling.

sentences.japanese: フェミニズムの目的は、女性を縛る鎖を断つことです。「女性らしさを失う」ことを押し付けるのではなく、「女性はこうあるべきだ」という抑圧への抵抗なんです。
sentences.english: The goal of feminism is to sever the chains that bind women. It is not about forcing women to "lose their femininity," but about resisting the oppression of "this is how women are supposed to be.”

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means divide so the verb vocab version is to divide or to split something . It can also mean to break something , as in ワイングラスを割る (to break a wine glass). After all, you’re technically dividing the object into parts if you break it, right?
readingMnemonic: The reading you learned with the kanji is the one you'll use here. It's the わ one, though, making it わる .

sentences.japanese: 七割る二の答えって、三余り一であってる？
sentences.english: Is the answer to "seven divided by two," three with a remainder of one?

sentences.japanese: ごめんなさい、お皿を割ってしまいました。
sentences.english: I’m sorry, I broke the plate.

sentences.japanese: コウイチは空手チョップで百枚の瓦を真っ二つに割ってみせた。
sentences.english: Koichi showed that he could break one hundred roofing tiles right in half with a karate chop.

meaningMnemonic: Election is 選挙 so when you make that word into a verb, you have to elect .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Also, the reading just comes from 選挙 so if you know that you know this as well.

sentences.japanese: トーフグの会長を毎年選挙しています。
sentences.english: We elect a Tofugu Chairman every year.

sentences.japanese: 政府は次のリーダーを選挙する日を発表しました。
sentences.english: The government announced the date for electing the next leader.

sentences.japanese: うちの学校では、毎年、生徒会長を選挙するイベントがあります。
sentences.english: Every year at our school, there's an event to elect the student council president.

meaningMnemonic: You escape and run the hell out of there. Basically, you're trying to escape , to flee , or to break out . Pretty simple. 脱走する specifically refers to escaping from a controlled or confined environment, like escaping from prison, a military base, or a guarded facility.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The だつ changes to だっ , though, so be careful of that.

sentences.english: to escape from a facility

sentences.japanese: 犯罪者が脱走する
sentences.english: to have a criminal escape

sentences.english: to have a cat escape

sentences.japanese: 兵士が脱走する
sentences.english: to have a soldier desert

sentences.japanese: 収容所を脱走する
sentences.english: to escape from a detention center

sentences.japanese: 施設を脱走する
sentences.english: to escape from a facility

sentences.japanese: 軍を脱走する
sentences.english: to desert from the military

sentences.japanese: 病院を脱走する
sentences.english: to escape from a hospital

sentences.japanese: どうやって脱走に成功したの？
sentences.english: How did you manage to break out?

sentences.japanese: 犬が脱走しないように、フェンスを作りました。
sentences.english: We built a fence to prevent the dog from escaping.

sentences.japanese: うちの子、学校から脱走しようとしたみたいなんだよね。
sentences.english: Apparently, our kid has tried to escape from school.

sentences.japanese: 重い刑罰を言い渡された犯罪者が、刑務所から脱走した。
sentences.english: The criminal, who had received a heavy sentence, broke out of prison.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means excel so the verb vocab version is to excel .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: " He-e ( ひい ) is going to excel ," you stutter. "He-e is!"

sentences.japanese: この大学には、一芸に秀でる学生は別ルートで入学することができる。
sentences.english: Students who excel in a particular field can enter this university through a different route.

sentences.japanese: サトミは、自分の考えを表現することに秀でている。
sentences.english: Satomi excels at expressing her thoughts.

sentences.japanese: 私は鼻くそをほじくることだけには秀でています。実際、鼻血を出すはめになったこともありません。
sentences.english: The only thing I excel at is picking my nose. In fact, I have never made my nose bleed.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. If you obtain something, you'll want it to fit inside your bag. Otherwise how can you take it home? When talking about problems or emotions, this verb can also mean to settle down and to be finished like a dispute settling down or someone’s anger calming down. Like most verbs with まる as okurigana, this is an intransitive verb. That means it happens by itself, with no emphasis on the person or thing that's making something fit inside, or settle down.
readingMnemonic: Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading. You haven't learned this reading yet so here's a mnemonic to help you: You don't fit inside your bed anymore. I guess you've grown? Better get out the trusty o ld saw s ( おさ ) and chop off your footboard.

sentences.japanese: 一億円、そのスーツケースに収まった？
sentences.english: Did the one hundred million yen fit inside the suitcase?

sentences.japanese: なんとか予算内に収まりそうです。
sentences.english: It looks like we'll somehow manage to stay within the budget.

sentences.japanese: アイスを食べたら、感情が収まってきたんだよね。
sentences.english: After eating the ice cream, my emotions started to settle down.

sentences.japanese: 大きいピザを五枚食べ切りたかったが、食べ放題の時間内に収まらなかった。
sentences.english: I wanted to eat all five large pizzas, but they couldn't be finished within the all-you-can-eat time limit.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji is descend , but this verb vocab word is to get off , as in, to get off the train, or to get out of the car. If you think about trains back in the day, you had to descend down to the platform to get out of them, which is how this word became what it is. You know that this word is the "to get off" word because once you get off the train, you enter the real ( りる ) world, where hardships are real and not as comfy as the train. Figuratively, this word also means to step down , as in "to give up" or "to resign” from something. For example, you can say ニュース番組を降りる (to step down from a news program) or ゲームを降りる (to drop out of a game).
readingMnemonic: The reading is unlike anything you've seen with this kanji. Just think about how you have to get off at O -station. None of the other letters are your stop. Just O -Station ( お ).

sentences.japanese: バスから降りるときは、気をつけてください。
sentences.english: Be careful when getting off the bus.

sentences.japanese: タクシーを降りる前に、忘れ物がないか確認しました。
sentences.english: Before getting out of the taxi, I checked to make sure I hadn't left anything behind.

sentences.japanese: 次の駅で降りるので、準備してください。
sentences.english: We're getting off at the next station, so please get ready.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji means "come true" or grant , and this is the transitive verb version of that, making this to grant or to fulfill . 叶える refers to making something desired come true, either for oneself or someone else. It's usually used in the context of fulfilling wishes, dreams, or goals, but it can also be used for granting someone's request in more formal contexts.
readingMnemonic: This is a verb, so it uses the kun'yomi reading. Luckily, you already learned this with the kanji, so you should be good to go here!

sentences.japanese: 夢を叶える
sentences.english: to fulfill a dream

sentences.japanese: 願いを叶える
sentences.english: to fulfill a wish, to grant someone's request

sentences.japanese: 希望を叶える
sentences.english: to fulfill a hope, to grant someone's request

sentences.japanese: 目標を叶える
sentences.english: to achieve a goal

sentences.japanese: ゼッタイにこの夢を叶えるんだ！
sentences.english: I will make this dream come true no matter what!

sentences.japanese: あなたは、いつまでにその目標を叶えたいですか？
sentences.english: When do you want to achieve that goal by?

sentences.japanese: 全ての希望を叶えることはできないかもしれません。
sentences.english: It may not be possible to fulfill all your wishes.

meaningMnemonic: Remember how 増える is "to increase" (as in, something just increases, you aren't doing the increasing yourself). This one is that one, where you're doing the increasing. So, this word means to increase something . You know you're doing the increasing because you said "yes" ( やす ) to increasing something, and did it yourself.
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same like 増える . If you know that vocab word you probably can read this one as well.

sentences.japanese: もっと文才のあるライターを増やすべきだ。
sentences.english: We really should increase the number of writers who have some literary talent.

sentences.japanese: トーフグのファンをもっと増やしたいんだけど、どうしたらいいかな？
sentences.english: We want to increase the number of Tofugu fans. What do you think we should do?

sentences.japanese: 平日に家族と過ごす時間を増やすために、宿題は全部週末にやることにしてるんだ。
sentences.english: I save all my homework for the weekend so I can spend more time with my family on weekdays.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means judge so the verb version is to judge .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: When you go to judge people, there are different types. The one you truly hate the most, however, is the sobber ( さば ). "The Sobber" is the worst kind. They just sob and sob and sob and it's really hard to move on to your next judging.

sentences.japanese: 裁判ではできるだけ公平に裁く必要があります。
sentences.english: In a trial it's necessary to judge as fairly as possible.

sentences.japanese: きっとアイツの罪は最高裁判所で裁かれるさ。
sentences.english: Surely his crime will be judged by the Supreme Court.

sentences.japanese: 折角あの男が殺人犯だとが分かったのに、時効を迎えているせいで法的には誰もヤツを裁く事ができないんだ。
sentences.english: It finally came out that the man is a murderer, but the statute of limitations has run out, so no one can legally try him.

meaningMnemonic: Remember how you learned that 心得 means "knowledge"? Well the verb version of that is to know . (You know it deep in your heart.)
readingMnemonic: The readings for this word are both kun'yomi readings. You've learned both of these readings by now so you should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: このお方をどなたと心得るか。
sentences.english: Does anyone know who this woman is?

sentences.japanese: その件についてはよく心得ております。
sentences.english: I'm well aware of the matter.

sentences.japanese: クック船長はクックパッドの使い方をよく心得ている。
sentences.english: Captain Cook knows how to use Cookpad very well.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means lead so the verb vocab version is to lead .
readingMnemonic: The reading for this one is a bit difficult, but there's a hint in the kanji. See the 道 in there on the top? What's the reading for the vocab version of that kanji? It's みち . That's the first part. Now, who are you leading? Let's say you're leading a bee back to its nest, via the road. It's a 道 Bee ( みちび )!

sentences.japanese: 生徒達を正しい道に導くのが教師の仕事だろ？
sentences.english: Isn't it the teacher's job to guide their students on the right path?

sentences.japanese: あのボクサーは、言葉で相手をイライラさせて、対戦相手を反則負けに導いた。
sentences.english: The boxer taunted his opponent with words, causing the opponent to lose by foul play.

sentences.japanese: あなたは父のことを誤解していると思います。彼は決して誰かを凶悪犯罪へと導くような人ではありません。
sentences.english: I think you misunderstand my father. He’s not the type of person who would lead someone into committing a heinous crime.

meaningMnemonic: If 演 is performance then the verb version of this would be to perform .
readingMnemonic: The reading looks weird, but it's actually just the reading you learned with the kanji.

sentences.japanese: 「演ずる」は「演じる」の、よりフォーマルな表現です。
sentences.english: "Enzuru" is a more formal expression for "enjiru."

sentences.japanese: 尻尾で喜びを示す犬の役を演ずるのがどんなに大変なことか、あなたは分かってらっしゃらないようですね。
sentences.english: You seem to not understand how difficult it is to play the role of a dog that expresses joy with its tail.

sentences.japanese: この度、私は、次のYoutubeビデオで、アメリカ大統領という大役を演ずることになりました。
sentences.english: I am excited to announce that I have been chosen to play the pivotal role of the United States President in our next YouTube video.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means provide so the verb vocab version is to provide .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You have to provide your friends with their own sauna ( そな ) because they don't want to use your shower. This requires you to go out and buy a sauna for your house (very expensive) just so you can provide your needy friends with what they want (a sauna). Feel angry you have to provide this.

sentences.japanese: 老後に備えて、家をバリアフリーにしました。
sentences.english: To prepare for our old age, we had our house renovated to be wheelchair-accessible.

sentences.japanese: トーフグのオフィスに電話が備え付けられましたが、ほとんどだれも使っていません。
sentences.english: The Tofugu office was equipped with a telephone, but hardly anybody uses it.

sentences.japanese: 気持ちを引き締めて敵の攻撃に備えろ！
sentences.english: Brace yourself and prepare for your opponent’s attack!

sentences.japanese: 休日って仕事に備えるためのものだと思ってました。自分が楽しむために使ってもいいんですね！
sentences.english: I used to think days off were for preparing for work. I see now it's okay to use them to enjoy myself!

meaningMnemonic: The kanji means raise , and this verb is when you do that to something. It's transitive. So this means to raise something . It actually has a pretty wide meaning, and can also mean "raise" in the sense of to cite something , like an example. It can even mean to hold something , like an event.
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as 挙がる , so if you know that reading you should know this one as well.

sentences.japanese: 例を挙げるとキリがないですよ。
sentences.english: If I were to give examples, it would be endless.

sentences.japanese: 名前を呼んだら、手を挙げてください。
sentences.english: When I call your name, please raise your hand.

sentences.japanese: 私は結婚式を市役所で挙げましたが、そのことを恥ずかしいとは思っていません。
sentences.english: I held my wedding ceremony in city hall, and I’m not ashamed of that.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means stretch , and the verb version means to stretch over something , to spread out , or to be taut , not to be confused with the type of stretching you do after a workout. This word is both transitive and intransitive. When it follows を , it emphasizes the physical act of extending something over an area, like stretching a canvas over a frame, unfurling a sail on a ship, or roping off a crime scene. When following が , it expresses the resulting state of having been stretched or spread, like a bloated stomach, a swollen muscle, or a spider web.
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You've got something you want to stretch over something else. Maybe it's some stretchy fabric or a rubber band or something. Whatever the case, everyone tells you it's going to break — but you manage to do it! " Hah ( は )! I knew I could pull it off! Hah!"

sentences.japanese: キャンバスをフレームに張る方法を教わりました。
sentences.english: I was taught how to stretch a canvas over a frame.

sentences.japanese: バレーボールのネットを張ったのは誰ですか？
sentences.english: Who put up the volleyball net?

sentences.japanese: テントをもうちょっとピンと張りたいんですが、手伝ってくれませんか？
sentences.english: I'd like to stretch the tent more tightly. Could you help me?

sentences.japanese: 久々にジョギングしたから、足がパンパンに張ってる。
sentences.english: I went jogging for the first time in a while, so my legs are swollen and tense.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember: When you cut the tree down to produce a tree trunk , out jumps Mickey Mouse. "WHY YOU CUT DOWN MY TREE BRO?" he yells. I'm Mickey Mouse and I don't stand for this.

sentences.japanese: 誰だ、幹にキズを付けたのは。
sentences.english: Who scratched the tree trunk?!

sentences.japanese: その木の幹をなでた時、木のさびしさにふれた気がしたんです。
sentences.english: When I rubbed the tree trunk, I felt as if I’d touched the loneliness of the tree.

sentences.japanese: 木の幹に絡まっているツタを取り除いた方がいいよ。
sentences.english: You should remove the ivy winding around the tree trunk.

meaningMnemonic: You're going to get judge d times two. Judge and judge again. Once by the judge and another time by the jury. This is a whole trial here.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You hopefully learned this on'yomi for 判 with the word 評判 , but here's a mnemonic to help you just in case: After your ban ( ばん ) on the WaniKani forums, you now face trial before none other than Judge Koichi. He's going to decide whether your ban will be lifted or not. Good luck, there's a lot at stake.

sentences.japanese: できるだけ、裁判はしたくないんですよね。
sentences.english: I'd like to avoid a trial, if possible.

sentences.japanese: 裁判の費用がいくらぐらいかかるか知っていますか？

You haven't learned that yet for 節 , so here's a mnemonic to help you remember it: The real turning point in your life was when you got yourself a few she ep ( ふし ). Owning a few sheep was a true milestone for you. Now you have all the wool sweaters and cheese you could ever want!

meaningMnemonic: When the status of your employment is " nothing " then you're probably unemployed . You're experiencing unemployment .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

meaningMnemonic: An element of clear up (like the sky clearing up!) is so wonderful and splendid . Sort of a weird word, but very useful. Just think of that wonderful feeling you get when the sun breaks and things clear up and it's awesome.
readingMnemonic: The reading is a bit weird, too. Luckily, you've learned both of them already. 晴れる is はれる . That's the reading you use here, though は goes to ば .
